qs.q: Why is Triple Negative Breast Cancer considered the most difficult to target therapeutically?
o: It only responds to high doses of tamoxifen
It lacks estrogen, progesterone, and HER2 receptors
It lacks a blood supply due to excessive desmoplasia
It is always discovered only after brain metastasis
qs.e: Triple negative breast cancer lacks ER, PR, and HER2 receptors, meaning neither hormone-blocking drugs nor trastuzumab will work, leaving chemotherapy as the only targeted option. The other choices do not accurately describe its receptor status.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which genetic mutation is most commonly associated with Triple Negative Breast Cancer and early-onset disease in young women?
qs.e: TNBC is most common in young women, women of African descent, and those with BRCA1 gene mutations. PIK3CA mutations are typically associated with the luminal cancer pathway.
qs.s: Breast Carcinoma: Understanding Types, Receptors & Treatment — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a high-grade triple-negative breast cancer. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal a germline mutation in which of the following genes?
o: Germline mutation in the BRCA1 gene
Germline mutation in the BRCA2 gene
Germline mutation in the CDH1 gene
Germline mutation in the CHEK2 gene
qs.e: Germline BRCA1 mutations are strongly associated with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and basal-like molecular subtypes. In contrast, BRCA2 mutations typically give rise to ER-positive, luminal tumors.

qs.q: Triple-negative breast carcinoma is defined by the absence of which three markers?
o: CA-125, HER2, and p53 protein expression
Ki-67, p53, and oestrogen receptor expression
Oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2
qs.e: Triple-negative breast cancer lacks ER, PR, and HER2. It has the worst prognosis among molecular subtypes and is strongly associated with BRCA1 mutations.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Triple‑negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks estrogen, progesterone and HER2 receptors, making it aggressive but treatable with chemotherapy. It often associates with BRCA1 mutations and basal‑like features.

sections.p: TNBC is defined by immunohistochemistry showing negative estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2/neu (IHC 0/1+ or 2+ with no amplification).

t.b: Determines receptor status; negative results confirm TNBC
Rules out HER2 amplification when IHC 2+; negative confirms TNBC

sections.p: TNBC follows the same TNM staging as other breast cancers. Prognosis depends on stage, grade and nodal involvement.
b: Stage I–IV based on tumour size, nodal status, metastasis

sections.p: Genetic predisposition (BRCA1), high proliferation, basal‑like gene expression. Environmental factors are less defined.
Patients present with a palpable mass, often in younger women. Skin changes, nipple retraction or ulceration may occur.
Beyond receptor testing, imaging and staging work‑up are essential.

t.b: Detects mass and architectural distortion; negative in dense breasts
Characterises solid vs cystic lesions; guides biopsy
Assesses extent in dense tissue or high‑risk patients
Determines nodal status; negative nodes reduce adjuvant therapy

sections.p: Rapid progression, visceral metastases, and treatment‑related toxicities are concerns.
b: Early metastasis to lungs, liver, brain

sections.p: Primary treatment is cytotoxic chemotherapy; surgery and radiotherapy are adjuncts based on stage.

t.b: Addresses systemic disease; chosen for high proliferation
Lumpectomy or mastectomy based on tumour size and patient preference
Reduces local recurrence after breast‑conserving surgery

sections.p: Regular imaging and clinical exams; genetic counselling for BRCA1/2.
Other high‑grade breast cancers like HER2‑positive or luminal B.
False‑negative HER2 IHC can occur; low tumour cellularity may mask receptor expression.

sections.p: Urgent care needed for sudden pain, rapid swelling, or neurological deficits indicating metastasis.

faq.a: Early‑stage TNBC can be cured with surgery, radiation and chemotherapy; advanced disease has poorer outcomes.
TNBC lacks hormone receptors, so endocrine agents are ineffective.

faq.q: Is BRCA1 the only genetic link?
faq.a: BRCA1 is common, but other genes (PALB2, ATM) can also predispose.
